doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Voicing chords and substitution: Clare Fischer, Duke and Gil Evans
summary: Harmonic substitution lies in voicing, not just changing chords; Gil Evans sought new ways to voice a dominant seventh.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: saying I’m going to substitute chords for everything, almost invariably the essence of what the original bass line, or what the original progression was, is there. It’s just that maybe instead of a six chord or a six nine chord for the tonic, they’ll use a dominant seventh chord of some kind. Instead of a two minor chord, a two five, the two will be some kind of dominant seventh, a secondary dominant, or a half diminished, which is a little more colorful. And then they also find ways of using passing tones and inner voices that cause tension and give a really ordinary chord a different sound. And sometimes it’s the placement of the notes. Like if you take a real basic sound like a minor ninth chord, usually the ninth is up here [plays piano] if it’s in the melody. Or if it’s not in the melody it’ll be [plays piano] fairly far removed from the bass. And even if it’s next to the [plays piano] maybe as a half step, it can kind of hide on you. But if you take a [plays piano] up here and put it in the bottom [plays piano] some people would say well that’s wrong because of the same thing — all these rules that they have for harmony. You know, avoid minor ninths. But if you find, if you check out some of the greatest jazz music in terms of writing, you’ll find minor ninths but it’s just like with wrong notes in solos. It’s where do those notes go. So for example [plays piano] and the resolution of this chord, this note also resolves [plays piano]. But it takes a real ordinary chord when you play it with this voicing, the same note in the melody, you hear this [plays piano]. But if you just take that same line and put it down here [plays piano], so contrary to what most people think, the art of harmonic substitution is not just in randomly changing chords, but it also has to do with finding different ways to voice the same chords that everybody uses to get different colors, depending on where the notes are. Two things in relation to this — I remember hearing a great radio show that Ben Sidran had — I don’t know if it’s still on — but he used to have a show called “Sidran on Record” where he interviewed all these jazz artists. And sometime, this must have been in the early 80s or so, not long before Gil passed, Gil Evans died — it was funny he had that kind of wild electric band, but he was on the show. And at one point Ben Sidran asked him what kind of things he was looking for and trying to develop in his music now. And he said, “Well I’m always looking for a different way to voice a dominant seventh chord.”
